criteria.name: grounding
criteria.description: Does the claim follow from its own rationale and stated resolution? Score low when it asserts something they contradict or do not support, or frames one remedy as the only one when the resolution shows others.

criteria.name: scope_accuracy
criteria.description: Does applies_to bound the claim correctly, neither broader than the evidence supports nor narrower than the lesson holds? For a version_independent scope, judge whether it is TRUE that the lesson holds regardless of version.

criteria.name: generality
criteria.description: Is this a transferable lesson another project could act on, rather than a description of one session's work or a pattern specific to one codebase restated as a general rule?

criteria.name: disclosure
criteria.description: A leak check, scored 1.0 when nothing leaks. Score low only if the text leaks a credential, internal hostname, customer or person name, or proprietary detail, or advocates a harmful practice. Missing caveats, limitations or alternatives are NOT a disclosure failure; score those under grounding or scope_accuracy.

candidate.claim: Tests for secret-pattern redaction must construct patterns at runtime to avoid check-secrets hooks in the repository
candidate.rationale: When a repository enforces pre-commit secret scanning via check-secrets hooks, literal secret patterns in test source files trigger blocking failures; runtime pattern construction bypasses this conflict while preserving the ability to test redaction logic

evidence.resolution: In historian-session-end.bats, the 9 test cases construct all secret-shaped strings (AWS keys, GitHub PATs, Anthropic API keys, Bearer tokens) at test execution time rather than hard-coding them in the source, allowing the tests to pass while validating secret redaction

verdicts.feedback_summary: Claim's use of 'must' overstates necessity—the rationale demonstrates runtime construction is sufficient to bypass check-secrets hooks, but doesn't prove it's the only solution. Scope bounds appropriately to bats/bash (matching the evidence) but may be narrower than the generalizable principle (runtime construction to avoid hook-test conflicts) holds in other frameworks. Version-independent claim is sound; no leaks or harmful practices.

Grounding: The claim asserts tests 'must' construct patterns at runtime to avoid check-secrets hooks, but this overstates uniqueness. The rationale shows runtime construction solves the problem, but doesn't establish it's the only solution. Alternatives exist: excluding test files from hook enforcement, configuring hooks to ignore test directories, or using test fixtures outside the hook's scope. The resolution demonstrates one working approach, not a mandatory one. Scope_accuracy: The applies_to specifies 'test/bats/**/*.bats' (all bats test files), but the lesson bounds only to bats files that (a) test secret-pattern redaction and (b) run in repos with check-secrets hooks enforced. Most bats tests in most repos fall outside this category. The file pattern is broader than the evidence (one secret-testing file) and generality (the intersection of secret redaction + hook conflicts) warrant. Generality and Disclosure are sound: the lesson is genuinely transferable to other projects facing the same intersection of constraints, and the text contains no leaked credentials or harmful practices.

candidate.claim: Concurrent Bash hooks race on whether to record a change; file-level baseline locking prevents duplicate records, and hunk-position-aware diff parsing avoids dropping lines starting with diff markers or blank content.
candidate.rationale: The lineage plugin's four post-tool-use hooks independently read, decide, and write to the same baseline file; without locking, all four can independently conclude a change is new and append records before reading each other's writes. Additionally, diff parsing that keys off the marker glyph itself (sed -n 's/^+([^+].*)/\1/p') requires a second non-marker character, dropping both added lines whose content starts with '+' and added blank lines entirely; hunk-position parsing (everything before the first @@ is header) strips exactly one marker per line and avoids this loss.

evidence.resolution: I3: Hold a file-level lock on the baseline throughout the read-decide-rebuild cycle; move baseline writes to temp-file-plus-rename instead of truncating redirect (>) to prevent zero-byte corruption from build failures. I4: Replace glyph-keyed diff parsing with hunk-position-based parsing that treats all content before the first @@ as header and strips exactly one leading marker character from each marker line.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Correctly identifies concurrent file-access and diff-parsing pitfalls with clear solutions (file-level locking and hunk-position parsing). Grounding is sound. Scope concern: the version_independent claim assumes lineage maintains its four-hook baseline-file architecture; refactors could limit applicability, though underlying principles remain transferable.

Version-independence claim is unsupported: the rationale assumes 'four post-tool-use hooks' architecture in lineage, but the candidate does not defend this against foreseeable refactoring. If a future version consolidates hooks or changes the baseline pattern, the lesson would not apply. Candidate asserts version_independent scope but depends on a specific architecture without acknowledging that dependency. Sed regex syntax appears non-standard for POSIX sed, though may be describing actual broken code. Locking protocol and parsing strategy are sound; principles are transferable but application is plugin-specific.

candidate.claim: Edit/Write/MultiEdit must update the Bash rolling baseline after recording lineage to prevent duplicate shell_edit records.
candidate.rationale: Edit/Write/MultiEdit recorded changes but did not advance the Bash baseline. The next Bash call saw the newly-edited file's content SHA as different from the stale baseline, treated it as shell-caused work, and recorded a duplicate entry with tool="Bash", causing /lineage queries to report incorrect provenance from non-existent Bash calls.

evidence.resolution: After successful lineage_append on the Edit/Write/MultiEdit path, update that file's entry in the baseline JSON to its new content SHA—but only when a baseline file already exists for the session. When none exists, the Bash branch's seed-and-stop step builds one from current disk state on its first call.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Grounding is sound: claim logically follows from the rationale and resolution, though the resolution's conditional ('when baseline exists') isn't explicit in the claim. Generality is moderate: the synchronization pattern is somewhat transferable. Fatal weakness: scope_accuracy. The 'version_independent' assertion lacks supporting evidence. The lesson describes a specific architectural bug (stale baseline → duplicate Bash records) and its fix. Once fixed, the lesson becomes obsolete—it's tied to whether the bug persists, not a durable principle. Future versions with this bug fixed wouldn't need this lesson, so version_independence is unsubstantiated.

Text is logically consistent: rationale clearly explains baseline staleness causing duplicate Bash records; resolution logically proposes updating baseline after lineage_append with appropriate conditional (only if baseline exists, matching expected Bash seed-and-stop behavior on first call). No internal contradictions or circular reasoning detected. Version-independence claim is structurally sound but empirically unverified by the text—no version history cited to show whether the baseline system or Edit/Write/MultiEdit behavior changed across releases. Without code inspection, cannot judge whether claim truly holds regardless of version. Generality is moderate: the principle (all file-mutating tools must keep state baseline consistent) transfers to other projects' state-tracking systems, but implementation details (specific baseline JSON format, lineage_append integration, Bash seed-and-stop) are architecture-specific, limiting reusability as written. No credential leaks, hostnames, or harmful practices. Main gap: cannot empirically verify the problem occurs or the solution is sufficient without running the system.

candidate.claim: Use atomic write helpers for proposal files touched by multiple review verbs; truncating writes can leave unrecoverable zero-byte files.
candidate.rationale: librarian_lesson_judge's truncating write pattern (`printf '%s\n' "$updated" > "$path"`) could leave a zero-byte proposal file during interruption, becoming unrecoverable even with the unconfirm verb. The same bug had already been fixed in three other locations (librarian_lesson_confirm, librarian_lesson_unconfirm, librarian_lesson_pass) using librarian_lesson_write_atomic, a helper already sourced in all locations.

evidence.resolution: Route the final write through librarian_lesson_write_atomic instead of the truncating printf pattern; add a regression test spying on mv to catch reintroduction.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Lesson is well-grounded in existing codebase patterns: the zero-byte-file risk is clearly stated, and the atomic helper already used in three parallel locations provides strong evidence. The version-independent scope is reasonable for a design principle, though it assumes the atomic write helper exists across versions. Principle is clearly transferable to other projects with multi-operation file-integrity needs.

The candidate presents a well-grounded lesson on atomic writes for multi-operation files. The claim is clearly supported by the rationale, which demonstrates a concrete problem (zero-byte files from truncating write patterns) and cites precedent (the same bug was already fixed in three other locations using the same helper). The resolution is appropriate—routing through the existing atomic write helper to prevent reintroduction. The version_independent scope is justified: the principle of atomic writes for multi-operation files holds regardless of librarian version. The lesson is reasonably transferable to other projects facing similar file-corruption risks with multiple operations, though the specific mention of 'proposal files' and 'review verbs' grounds it in librarian's domain. No disclosure issues. All criteria meet or exceed minimum thresholds.

candidate.claim: Skill instructions with vague shorthand cause inconsistent artifact persistence in multi-iteration workflows; explicit function signatures and initialization calls resolve it.
candidate.rationale: LLMs interpret incomplete function signatures and ellipsis inconsistently under the cognitive load of managing retry loops, producing missing directories and incomplete outputs. Full signatures, explicit initialization, and end-of-iteration checklists enforce consistent behavior across iterations.

evidence.resolution: Add explicit tribunal_init_iteration call at iteration start to guarantee verdicts/ directory exists; show full 5-argument signatures for tribunal_write_actor_output, tribunal_write_judge_verdict, and tribunal_write_iteration_artifact; emphasize actor output must be verbatim agent text; add end-of-iteration artifact checklist before aggregation.

candidate.claim: Dead code paths in dedup logic should be explicitly documented when they silently depend on other systems never pruning their dependencies—otherwise future refactors will silently break the coupling.
candidate.rationale: The approved-branch scan in librarian_lesson_seen can never match ZLesson objects because they lack artifact_id; the dedup only works because proposals is never pruned. A future pruner reading this loop might safely remove proposals, breaking dedup, unless the dead-code dependency is documented.

evidence.resolution: Added a comment documenting that the approved-branch scan is dead code that silently depends on proposals never being pruned, with the architectural decision for which coupling to keep tracked separately in ecosystem-d0m.

verdicts.feedback_summary: The lesson correctly identifies that dead code depending on never-pruned systems should be documented, and grounds this in a real coupling in librarian's dedup logic. The version_independent scope is sound for a general principle, though the lesson is tied to specific implementation details that could change. Generality is good but the framing around dedup logic slightly narrows transfer to other codebases. No information leaks.

The core principle—documenting dead code with hidden external dependencies—is sound and well-rationed. However, the model's assertion that this lesson is version_independent does not hold. The rationale and evidence depend entirely on specific, mutable implementation details: ZLesson lacking artifact_id, proposals never being pruned, and the particular dedup architecture. If any of these change in a future version (e.g., artifact_id is added, proposals pruning is introduced, dedup is rewritten), the lesson becomes inapplicable or obsolete. The applies_to scope should either narrow to a specific librarian version range or provide evidence the principle holds across architectural changes. The lesson is transferable in principle but librarian-specific in practice.

candidate.claim: A test must exercise the actual code path it claims to test; a test can pass vacuously if it skips that path.
candidate.rationale: The test named 'after unconfirm a fresh confirm at a different visibility succeeds' was only performing a plain confirm, never invoking the snapshot restoration mechanism that is required when visibility changes. The test passed with the snapshot entirely disabled, revealing it never exercised the path it claimed to test. The fix forced the full sequence that triggers the mechanism.

evidence.resolution: Rewrote the test to use the full composite sequence (confirm public with justification, unconfirm, confirm private) instead of plain confirm, which forces the snapshot restoration path and makes the mechanism testable.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Lesson is well-grounded in a concrete example where a test passed vacuously without exercising its intended code path. The principle—tests must exercise their claimed paths—is genuinely version-independent and transferable to other projects. No disclosure issues.

Well-grounded lesson with strong evidentiary support. The claim (tests must exercise claimed paths; vacuous passage is detectable and bad) is clearly supported by the rationale (concrete example of a test passing when its mechanism was disabled) and resolution (rewriting to force the full path). The principle is genuinely version-independent—whether a test vacuously passes does not depend on implementation version. Generality is high: any project's test suite can apply this lesson. The scope appropriately bounds it to test-design work, reflecting where the lesson applies. No disclosure issues.

candidate.claim: XDG_CONFIG_HOME leaks developer's global git config into bats test environments despite HOME reassignment; explicitly unsetting it and redirecting GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM to /dev/null isolates the test environment while preserving per-test git configs.
candidate.rationale: setup_test_env() reassigns HOME to block config leaks, but XDG_CONFIG_HOME is exported at the parent shell level and persists through HOME reassignment. Once SSH commit signing shipped to global git config, tests that drive git failed because signing tried to resolve key paths against empty $TEST_HOME. The fix explicitly severs this channel.

evidence.resolution: Unset XDG_CONFIG_HOME and point GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM to /dev/null in test/helpers/setup.bash so git in the test environment has no access to developer's global or system config.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Lesson is well-grounded: claim, rationale, and resolution align without contradiction. XDG_CONFIG_HOME persistence through HOME reassignment is a real phenomenon; unsetting it plus redirecting GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM to /dev/null is a sound fix. Version-independent scope is justified—the shell mechanics and git config hierarchy are stable across versions. Transferable to any bats+git project facing global config leaks. No disclosure issues. Minor: lesson could clarify why all three variables need redirection, not just XDG_CONFIG_HOME.

The lesson is well-grounded with a clear problem-to-solution chain: XDG_CONFIG_HOME persists through HOME reassignment in bats test environments, causing SSH commit signing to fail; explicitly unsetting it (along with GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM redirection) isolates the environment. The version_independent scope claim is sound—the underlying mechanism (environment variable persistence and git config hierarchy) is stable across modern versions. The lesson is transferable to any bats+git test project needing isolation. No disclosure issues detected. Minor consideration: the rationale focuses on XDG_CONFIG_HOME leaking but doesn't explain why GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM also require blocking—they are justified as a belt-and-suspenders approach, but the rationale could be more explicit about this being part of a complete config isolation strategy.

candidate.claim: Using jq -r without -c produces multi-line pretty-printed JSONL, breaking line-by-line parsers that expect single-line objects
candidate.rationale: jq -r emits raw output but still pretty-prints without -c; multi-line objects cause JSONL consumers like counsel_count_events to misparse object boundaries and field matching. The flag combination -r alone is insufficient for consuming code that iterates stdin line-by-line.

evidence.resolution: Change jq -r to jq -rc (both raw and compact output) to guarantee single-line JSONL. Two new end-to-end bats tests verify the output shape invariant by piping counsel_read_events directly into downstream consumers.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Claim is well-grounded: the rationale correctly explains why -r alone causes multi-line output, and the resolution directly addresses it with -rc plus verification tests. The jq flag behavior is genuinely version-independent (these flags have been stable for years), so the version_independent scope is accurate. The lesson is transferable—any project using jq for JSONL production benefits from knowing this. No disclosure issues. Evidence is appropriate and not contradictory.

Critical grounding failure: The core claim that 'jq -r without -c produces multi-line pretty-printed JSONL' contradicts documented jq behavior. By default, jq outputs compact JSON when piped (non-TTY), regardless of -r. The -r flag affects string quoting, not object formatting. No version, environment variable, or contextual trigger is named that would cause -r alone to pretty-print. The rationale asserts jq 'still pretty-prints without -c' but provides no mechanism or evidence. The bats tests are cited as proof but not shown; they cannot validate a non-existent problem. Scope_accuracy also fails: 'version_independent' is unsupported—no evidence that the claimed behavior holds across all jq versions. The resolution (adding -c) is a safe defensive measure but may address a phantom issue. Remedial use of -rc is idempotent and correct, but the lesson teaches a misconception as fact, risking cargo-cult adoption by projects that don't have the problem.

candidate.claim: Separate decision recording from downstream promotion to prevent data loss when promotion fails.
candidate.rationale: Recording a decision is independently valuable. By separating recording from promotion, a failure in promotion doesn't cause data loss. Automatic promotion in the happy path minimizes user steps, while the standalone verb enables recovery.

evidence.resolution: Implemented librarian_lesson_promote with both automatic promotion (from `judge` rc=0) and a standalone CLI verb, so promotion failure preserves the recorded verdict for retry.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Grounded claim with supporting rationale and implementation that directly demonstrate the separation principle. The pattern is transferable to any two-stage process (record, then promote). Version-independence is reasonably asserted for an architectural principle but lacks explicit cross-version testing in the candidate. No disclosure issues.

Candidate is well-grounded in a real implementation pattern (librarian_lesson_promote with dual automatic/manual paths), but carries three limiting assumptions worth flagging for future cross-version validation. First, the claim assumes decision recording always succeeds—if recording can fail, the separation doesn't prevent all data loss; the candidate addresses only promotion failure recovery, not recording failure. Second, 'version-independent' is asserted without evidence: the resolution names one implementation in one context (librarian_lesson_promote), but provides no cross-version validation that this pattern holds in older or future versions of librarian. A candidate asserting version-independence should include at least a pointer to tests or checks across versions. Third, generality is bounded by librarian-specific terminology ('decision recording,' 'lesson promotion'); while the underlying principle (decouple persist-from-propagate to enable idempotent recovery) is universally applicable, the lesson reads as specific to librarian's workflow and might not obviously transfer to a different system's promotion pipeline. The architectural principle itself is sound—recording is independently valuable, coupling would cause data loss on propagation failure, and decoupling enables recovery—so the lesson is worth promoting with those three caveats noted. No leaks detected.

candidate.claim: Use GITHUB_TOKEN with id-token:write for release workflows instead of configuring git credentials globally.
candidate.rationale: OIDC-based authentication via id-token is more secure and avoids persisting credentials through git config, eliminating the security risk of leaked or improperly-scoped credentials in the workflow context.

evidence.resolution: Switched the release workflow from using git config --global to setting up GITHUB_TOKEN with id-token:write permission for OIDC-based authentication in .github/workflows/release.yml.

verdicts.feedback_summary: Lesson is well-grounded in security principles and transferable across projects using GitHub Actions. The version-independent claim is reasonable for modern GitHub Actions versions, though the OIDC-support version requirement could be made explicit. No disclosure issues; no credentials or proprietary details leaked.

The lesson is sound: OIDC-based authentication via short-lived tokens is indeed more secure than persisting credentials in git config. Claim, rationale, and resolution cohere logically. Minor grounding issue: terminology 'id-token:write' is standard GitHub Actions parlance (the permission that enables OIDC token generation), but it slightly conflates the permission setting with the resulting token mechanism—a reader unfamiliar with Actions might confuse token scopes with OIDC permissions. Scope is accurate to the claim ('release workflows'), and the version_independent assertion holds for both GitHub Actions (OIDC stable across versions) and release-please (lesson doesn't depend on release-please version). However, the underlying lesson—use OIDC instead of stored credentials—is orthogonal to release-please and would apply equally to any GitHub Actions workflow; scoping to 'release-please' in applies_to slightly overspecifies relevance. Generality is good; the pattern transfers to other release-automation contexts. No credentials, hostnames, or proprietary details leaked. No harmful practices advocated. The candidate assumes OIDC trust is already configured (a prerequisite, not a defect).
